content: Dysmenorrhoea, characterized by painful menstrual cramps, is a prevalent gynecological condition. Conventional treatments typically involve non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and oral contraceptive pills (OCPs), both of which work by reducing uterine contractions (myometrial activity). Dietary supplements have been proposed as an alternative treatment option. These supplements include herbs, vitamins, minerals, enzymes, and amino acids, but traditional Chinese medicines were excluded from this analysis. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of dietary supplements in managing dysmenorrhoea. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, AMED, and PsycINFO, covering studies up to March 23, 2015. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving dietary supplements for moderate or severe primary or secondary dysmenorrhoea were included, while studies involving women with intrauterine devices were excluded. Comparators included other supplements, placebo, no treatment, or conventional analgesics. Two independent reviewers selected studies, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. Pain intensity and adverse effects were the primary outcomes. Statistical analyses were performed using fixed-effect models, and the quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE methodology. A total of 27 RCTs involving 3101 women were included. Most studies were conducted among young women with primary dysmenorrhoea, primarily in Iran and other middle-income countries. Only one study addressed secondary dysmenorrhoea. The interventions studied included 12 herbal supplements (e.g., German chamomile, cinnamon, Damask rose, dill, fennel, fenugreek, ginger, guava, rhubarb, uzara, valerian, and zataria) and five non-herbal supplements (fish oil, melatonin, vitamins B1 and E, and zinc sulfate) in various formulations and doses. Comparators included other supplements, placebo, no treatment, and NSAIDs. The overall quality of evidence was judged to be low or very low due to small sample sizes, poor reporting of study methods, and inconsistency in results. For primary dysmenorrhoea, the effectiveness of supplements compared to placebo or no treatment was inconsistent. For example: Vitamin E showed no evidence of effectiveness. Dill, guava, and fennel showed inconsistent or limited evidence of benefit. Fenugreek, fish oil, fish oil combined with vitamin B1, ginger, valerian, vitamin B1 alone, zataria, and zinc sulfate showed some evidence of effectiveness, but the quality of evidence was low. Data on chamomile and cinnamon were unsuitable for analysis. When compared to NSAIDs, there was no evidence of a difference in effectiveness for dill, fennel, guava, rhubarb, or valerian. There was limited evidence suggesting that chamomile might be more effective than NSAIDs. Comparisons between supplements (e.g., ginger vs. zinc sulfate, vitamin B1 vs. fish oil) showed mixed results, with vitamin B1 potentially being more effective than fish oil. For secondary dysmenorrhoea, there was no strong evidence of benefit for melatonin compared to placebo in cases of endometriosis-related pain. Regarding safety, only four studies reported adverse effects for both treatment and control groups. There was no evidence of a difference in safety between groups, but the data were too limited to draw definitive conclusions. In conclusion, there is no high-quality evidence to support the effectiveness of any dietary supplement for dysmenorrhoea. Evidence regarding safety is also insufficient. However, some low-quality evidence suggests potential benefits for certain supplements, warranting further research in this area.
